summary.heading: Pressure and the mole
summary.html:
$$P = \frac{F}{A} \qquad n = \frac{N}{N_A}$$
  • $F$ is the force perpendicular to the surface. Pressure is a scalar, in Pa ($1\ \text{Pa} = 1\ \text{N m}^{-2}$). Air pressure at sea level is about $1.0 \times 10^5$ Pa.
  • $N_A = 6.02 \times 10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$. Molar mass $M$: mass of one mole (in $\text{g mol}^{-1}$, numerically equal to the relative molecular mass), so $n = \dfrac{m}{M}$. Convert g to kg when needed.

summary.heading: The kinetic model of an ideal gas
summary.html:
• Assumptions: a very large number of identical molecules moving randomly with a range of speeds; their total volume is negligible; no forces except during collisions (straight lines at constant speed between them); perfectly elastic collisions; collisions take negligible time; Newton's laws apply.
  • No intermolecular forces means no potential energy: an ideal gas's internal energy is all kinetic.
  • Pressure: molecules bouncing off a wall change momentum, so the wall pushes on them and they push on the wall (Newton's 2nd and 3rd laws).
  • Heating at constant volume: faster molecules hit more often and harder, so $P$ rises. Compressing at constant temperature: same speed, but more frequent hits per square metre. Heating at constant pressure: the gas must expand.

summary.heading: The gas laws and the ideal gas equation
summary.html:
• For a fixed mass of gas: Boyle's law $PV = \text{constant}$ (constant $T$); Charles's law $\dfrac{V}{T} = \text{constant}$ (constant $P$); pressure law $\dfrac{P}{T} = \text{constant}$ (constant $V$). $T$ in kelvin.
  • Testing Boyle's law: plot $P$ against $\dfrac{1}{V}$ for a straight line through the origin. Wait for the gas to return to room temperature after each change.
$$\frac{P_1V_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2V_2}{T_2} \qquad PV = nRT = Nk_BT$$
  • $R = 8.31\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$ with moles; $k_B = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\ \text{J K}^{-1}$ with numbers of molecules. $R = N_Ak_B$.
  • $1\ \text{litre} = 1000\ \text{cm}^3 = 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3$.

summary.heading: Pressure from molecular collisions
summary.html:
$$P = \frac{1}{3}\rho v_{\text{rms}}^2$$
  • Outline: momentum change $2mu$ per collision; one hit every $\dfrac{2L}{u}$; force $\dfrac{mu^2}{L}$; a third of the motion in each direction; divide by area, and $\dfrac{Nm}{L^3} = \rho$. Know the idea and the result, not the full derivation.
  • New for 2028 rms speed: square the speeds, take the mean, then the square root. It is not the mean speed (100, 200, 300, 400 $\text{m s}^{-1}$: mean 250, rms 274), and it is never smaller (equal only if every molecule has the same speed).
  • New for 2028 The average velocity of the molecules is zero (random directions). The gas laws use the mean of $v^2$ because each molecule's effect on pressure (harder and more frequent hits) and its kinetic energy both depend on $v^2$.

summary.heading: Temperature, speed and internal energy
summary.html:
• Combining $PV = \frac{1}{3}Nmv_{\text{rms}}^2$ with $PV = Nk_BT$: $\tfrac{1}{2}mv_{\text{rms}}^2 = \tfrac{3}{2}k_BT$. Kelvin temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the molecules.
$$U = \frac{3}{2}Nk_BT = \frac{3}{2}nRT$$
  • For an ideal monatomic gas only. For a fixed amount of gas, $U$ depends only on temperature, not on pressure or volume.

summary.heading: Pressure–volume diagrams and real gases
summary.html:
• Two of $P$, $V$, $T$ fix the state, so a change of state is a line on a p–V diagram.
  • Isobaric: horizontal line. Isovolumetric: vertical line. Isothermal: a curve $PV = \text{constant}$ (an isotherm); hotter isotherms lie further from the origin.
  • Real gases: molecules have some volume and attract slightly, so real gases can liquefy. They behave nearly ideally at low pressure, low density and high temperature (well above liquefying).

summary.heading: Watch out for
summary.html:
• Using °C in any gas equation.
  • Leaving volumes in litres or cm³ in $PV = nRT$ (the ratio form only needs matching units, but $T$ must still be in K).
  • Mixing up $n$ with $R$ and $N$ with $k_B$.
  • Saying molecules hit harder when compressed at constant temperature. They hit more often.
  • Treating $v_{\text{rms}}^2$ as the square of the mean speed.
  • Using $U = \frac{3}{2}nRT$ for real or non-monatomic gases.
  • Applying the gas laws when gas leaks (the mass must be fixed).

Experiments and patterns: Give students Boyle-style data (pressure and volume of trapped air). How would they find the pattern, and what graph would convince a sceptic?

Boyle's law (1662) was used for nearly two centuries before the kinetic explanation was accepted (Bernoulli's 1738 explanation was largely ignored). Is a law with no accepted explanation still useful?
Models: Theory and experiment both reach $PV = nRT$. Which assumptions in the kinetic model were really guesses at the time?
Ask students which kinetic-model assumption they would drop first to make the model more realistic, and what it would change.
Shared endeavour: The same law was stated in different but equivalent ways by different scientists. How do scientists decide two statements say the same thing?
Avogadro's hypothesis was ignored for about 50 years. What had to change before it was accepted?
Ideal and real: Engineers designing a scuba tank or a gas pipeline need to know when "ideal" is good enough. How would they find out?
Is it a weakness or a strength of physics that it builds on things that don't exist, like ideal gases?

oracy.html:
ABC discussion (threes, 8 minutes): each student in turn agrees with, builds on or challenges the last point. Claim: "A sealed balloon shrinks in the freezer because the gas molecules get smaller when they are cold."

  • I agree with … because …
  • Building on that, …
  • I'd challenge that, because …

Listen for: the molecules stay the same size but move more slowly; at constant pressure the volume is proportional to the kelvin temperature, so cooling from 293 K to 255 K makes it about 13% smaller.

When is an idealised model \"good enough: Compare $PV = nRT$ with real data for air at room conditions and for CO2 near liquefaction. Where does "good enough" end?
Is knowing the limits of a model part of knowing the model?
Can we know that something exists before: Mach and Ostwald doubted atoms. Einstein's 1905 analysis of Brownian motion, confirmed by Perrin's measurements in 1908–09, changed most minds (Ostwald accepted atoms in 1909; Mach never did). Why were these measurements more convincing than the success of the gas laws?
Can we "see" atoms today with electron microscopes, or is that still an inference?
Do two routes to the same answer make it: If two independent methods agree, could they both share the same hidden mistake? Give an example.
Compare with other areas of knowledge: does a historian trust an event more when two independent sources agree?
Is a \"law\" in science the same as a la: A society's law can be broken and still be a law. Can a scientific law be broken and still be a law?
Should Boyle's law be renamed "Boyle's approximation"? What would be gained or lost?
